---
title: "Exponential"
description: "A long right tail recedes slowly"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("../R/populations.R")
source("../R/diagnostics.R")
source("../R/simulation.R")
source("../R/plots.R")
library(ggplot2)
population <- get_population("exponential")
diagnostics <- read.csv("../results/diagnostics.csv")
page_results <- diagnostics[diagnostics$population == "exponential", ]
bands <- read.csv("../results/calibration_bands.csv")
selected_n <- c(30, 300, 750)
simulation <- simulate_population(population, selected_n, B = 10000L, seed = 631L, keep_means = TRUE)
```

## 1. Question and prediction

The Exponential parent is continuous but strongly right-skewed. I expected the ordinary CLT to work, yet much more slowly than for the symmetric die because averaging must tame a long right tail.

## 2. Parent population

```{r}
#| label: fig-exponential-parent
#| fig-cap: "The rate-1 Exponential density concentrates near zero and extends to the right. This asymmetry is the feature averaging must overcome."
#| fig-alt: "A density curve highest at zero and decreasing with a long right tail."
plot_parent_population(population)
```

## 3. Theory before simulation

For $X_i \sim Exp(1)$, $E(X)=1$ and $Var(X)=1$. All ordinary CLT conditions hold, giving center 1 and theoretical standard error $1/\sqrt{n}$.

The exact sample sum is Gamma, so the remaining standardized skewness shrinks like $2/\sqrt{n}$. This predicts slow but steady progress.

## 4. Simulation design

The adaptive grid extends from $n=1$ to $n=1000$, with extra points between 75 and 500 where the skewness approaches the practical band. Every point uses 10,000 means and seed 631.

## 5. Numerical evidence

```{r}
#| label: tbl-exponential-diagnostics
#| tbl-cap: "Exponential diagnostics near the transition. Center and SE are accurate before the right-tail shape meets the practical skewness guidance."
shown <- page_results[page_results$n %in% c(100, 150, 200, 300, 500, 750), c("n", "mean_error", "relative_se_error", "skewness", "excess_kurtosis", "qq_rmse")]
names(shown) <- c("n", "Center error", "Relative SE error", "Skewness", "Excess kurtosis", "Q-Q RMSE")
knitr::kable(shown, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

At $n=300$, skewness is `r sprintf("%.3f", page_results$skewness[page_results$n == 300])` and relative SE error is `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * page_results$relative_se_error[page_results$n == 300])`. Q-Q RMSE remains above the exact-Normal noise band, so the graphical tail check still matters.

## 6. Shape across sample sizes

```{r}
#| label: fig-exponential-sampling
#| fig-cap: "At n = 30 the right tail is still visible. By n = 300 the sampling distribution is close enough to a symmetric bell for practical use, and n = 750 confirms continued stability."
#| fig-alt: "Three histograms centered near one, with right skew diminishing as sample size grows."
plot_sampling_distributions(simulation$means, population, selected_n)
```

## 7. Q-Q evidence

```{r}
#| label: fig-exponential-qq
#| fig-cap: "Right-tail Q-Q curvature is material at n = 30, modest at n = 300, and smaller at n = 750. The comparison shows why a tail diagnostic delays the conclusion."
#| fig-alt: "Three Q-Q panels with decreasing upward curvature in the right tail."
plot_qq_comparison(simulation$means, population, selected_n)
```

## 8. Diagnostic trajectory

```{r}
#| label: fig-exponential-trajectory
#| fig-cap: "Shape diagnostics generally decline with n but fluctuate under finite simulation. Skewness enters the practical band at n = 300 and remains modest at the next larger evaluations."
#| fig-alt: "Three line charts with declining skewness, kurtosis, and Q-Q error over a log sample-size axis."
plot_diagnostic_trajectory(page_results, population, bands)
```

## 9. Decision and disagreement

**Decision: $n=300$.** Center and SE have long since stabilized, skewness reaches the practical 0.10 band, and the remaining tail curvature is not large enough to misrepresent the main distribution. The judgment persists at $n=500$ and $n=750$. Q-Q RMSE remains stricter than the visual decision, which warns that sensitive extreme-tail work may still need more data.

## 10. Limitation and surprise

A single threshold cannot serve every tail probability. The most useful surprise is how early the mean and SE look correct compared with the shape: first and second moments alone would have declared victory much too soon.
